title: Pronoun case: I or me, who or whom
blurb: Choose I or me, we or us, who or whom, and myself only when it belongs, using two quick tests.
question: A nursing applicant writes, “Between you and I, my mentor and me were nervous, and the award went to Dr. Lin and myself.” How many pronoun case errors are there, and how would you fix each one?

teach.h: Case is the pronoun's job form
teach.body: Formally, case is the form a pronoun takes to show its job: subjective for a subject, objective for an object of a verb or preposition, and possessive for ownership. Plain English: “I” does things, “me” has things done to it or sits after a word like to, for or between. The HESI A2 hides the pronoun inside a pair (“Ana and me”) or after a preposition (“between you and I”) so your ear stops helping. The tests below put your ear back to work.

head: Subjective (does)
Objective (receives)
Possessive (owns)
teach.caption: Objective case after verbs (call me), prepositions (to, for, with, between, of) and infinitives (to help them). Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe: hers, its, yours, theirs.

steps.label: Read it alone
steps.sub: “Me went”? I went. “for I”? for me.

steps.label: Put the pair back
steps.sub: Ana and I went. For Ana and me.

teach.caption: The same test fixes we/us + noun: drop the noun. “(We) nurses agree.” “The memo was for (us) nurses.”

teach.h: Errors that sound polite but are wrong
teach.caption: Myself is correct only when it reflects an I in the same clause (“I reminded myself”) or adds emphasis (“I checked it myself”).

teach.h: Who vs whom: the he/him test
teach.body: Who is subjective, like he. Whom is objective, like him. Turn the pronoun's own clause into a statement and swap in he or him. “___ is on call?” He is on call, so who. “To ___ should I send it?” Send it to him, so whom. “Give it to ___ asks first”: inside its clause, he asks, so whoever, even though “to” comes before it. Ignore inserted phrases such as “do you think”: “Who do you think will win?” (he will win).

head: Sentence
Swap
Answer
teach.caption: In casual questions (“Who did you call?”) who is widely accepted; the HESI keys whom where the sentence is formal or the pronoun follows a preposition.

teach.body: Finish the comparison in your head. “Jada works more shifts than I (do)”: I is the subject of the unspoken verb, so the subjective form. When the verb is written out, the choice is clear: “than I have,” never “than me have.” Use the same move for as: “Leo is as tired as she (is).”

teach.h: Scenario: Marcus fixes his personal statement
teach.body: Applicant Marcus Reed drafts: “Between you and I, my mentor and me were nervous, and the award went to Dr. Lin and myself.” Fix 1: between is a preposition, so “between you and me.” Fix 2: drop test on the subject, “me were nervous” fails, so “my mentor and I.” Fix 3: myself has no I in its clause to reflect, and “to” needs the objective case, so “to Dr. Lin and me.” Three errors, three fixes.

teach.text: “Between you and I” and “whom” used as a subject (“the nurse whom answered”) both sound formal, which is exactly why the HESI A2 uses them. Formal-sounding is not the same as correct: check the job, then the case.

items: Subjective (I, we, he, she, they, who) for subjects; objective (me, us, him, her, them, whom) for objects of verbs and prepositions.
Pairs and we/us + noun: drop the other words and read the pronoun alone.
Who = he (subject); whom = him (object). Decide inside the pronoun's own clause.
Whoever is the subject of its own verb even after a preposition (to whoever asks).
Myself only reflects an I in the same clause or adds emphasis; never hisself or theirselves.
Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe: hers, its, ours, yours, theirs.

summary: You can now choose the right pronoun case with the drop test and the he/him test, including pairs, we/us before a noun, who/whom and whoever. You can also spot myself used as a polite substitute and possessive pronouns written with an apostrophe.

A.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “The charge nurse asked Kiara and ___ to restock the supply room.”
A.why: “Kiara and ___” is the object of “asked,” so the objective case is needed. Drop test: “asked me,” so “asked Kiara and me.”

whyNot.0: “I” is subjective; “asked I” fails the drop test.
whyNot.1: “Myself” is reflexive and needs an I earlier in the sentence; there is none.
whyNot.3: “She” is subjective; as an object of “asked” it would have to be “her.”

options: Whom is covering the night shift tonight?
To who should I send the incident report?
The nurse whom answered was very kind.
The patient to whom we spoke is here now.
A.why: The pronoun is the object of the preposition “to” (we spoke to him), so the objective “whom” is correct.

whyNot.0: The pronoun is the subject of “is covering” (he is covering), so it should be “Who.”
whyNot.1: After the preposition “to,” the objective “whom” is needed.
whyNot.2: The pronoun is the subject of “answered” (she answered), so it should be “who.”

A.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “The new policy was explained to ___ volunteers on Monday.”
A.why: Drop the noun: “explained to us.” The pronoun is the object of the preposition “to,” so the objective “us” is correct.

whyNot.0: “Explained to we” fails the drop test; “we” is subjective.
whyNot.2: “Ourselves” is reflexive and needs “we” as the subject of the clause.
whyNot.3: “Them” cannot point to a noun; “them volunteers” is nonstandard.

B.q: Which sentence uses the pronoun correctly?
options: Please send the schedule to Dr. Patel or myself.
Dr. Patel and myself will review the schedule.
I reminded myself to review the schedule.
The schedule was reviewed by Dr. Patel and I.
B.why: “Myself” correctly reflects the subject “I” in the same clause.

whyNot.0: There is no I for “myself” to reflect; the object of “to” should be “me.”
whyNot.1: “Myself” cannot be a subject; it should be “Dr. Patel and I.”
whyNot.3: After the preposition “by,” the objective “me” is needed: “by Dr. Patel and me.”

B.q: Which pair of pronouns correctly completes the sentence? “___ nursing applicants were told to arrive by 7:30 a.m., so the proctor checked IDs for ___ first.”
B.why: Drop the noun: “We were told” (subject, so we) and “for us” (object of a preposition, so us).

whyNot.0: Both are reversed: “Us were told” and “for we” both fail the drop test.
whyNot.2: “Us were told” fails: the subject needs “we.”
whyNot.3: “For we” fails: the object of “for” needs “us.”

B.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “Omar has finished more care plans this term than ___ have.”
B.why: The verb “have” is written out, so the pronoun is its subject: “than I have.”

whyNot.0: “Than me have” fails: “me” cannot be the subject of “have.”
whyNot.1: “Myself” is reflexive and cannot be the subject of “have.”
whyNot.3: “Her have” fails: the subject form is “she,” which would also need “has.”

C.q: Which revision corrects every pronoun error in this sentence? “Between you and I, Jordan and me were nervous before the exam.”
options: Between you and me, Jordan and I were nervous
Between you and I, Jordan and I were nervous
Between you and me, Jordan and me were nervous
Between you and myself, Jordan and I were nervous
C.why: “Between” is a preposition, so “me” (objective). “Jordan and ___ were nervous” is a subject, so “I” (subjective).

whyNot.1: Fixes the subject but leaves “between you and I,” which needs the objective “me.”
whyNot.2: Fixes the preposition but leaves “Jordan and me were,” which needs the subjective “I.”
whyNot.3: “Myself” has no I to reflect; after “between,” use “me.”

C.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “Give the extra parking pass to ___ arrives first tomorrow.”
C.why: The pronoun is the subject of “arrives” inside its own clause (he arrives), so the subjective “whoever” is correct. The whole clause is the object of “to.”

whyNot.0: “Whomever” is objective, but the pronoun is the subject of “arrives”; the preposition governs the whole clause, not the pronoun.
whyNot.1: “Whom” is objective and cannot be the subject of “arrives.”
whyNot.3: “Who's” means “who is”: “to who is arrives” makes no sense.

C.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “The applicant with ___ the committee spoke first was offered a seat.”
C.why: The pronoun is the object of the preposition “with” (the committee spoke with him), so the objective “whom” is correct.

whyNot.0: “Who” is subjective; directly after the preposition “with,” the objective “whom” is needed.
whyNot.2: “Whose” shows possession and would need a noun after it (whose essay).
whyNot.3: “Which” refers to things, not to a person such as an applicant.

reteach.title: Pronouns wear job badges
reteach.question: Think of each pronoun as a worker who wears a badge for the job they are doing right now. How do you know which badge to hand out?

blocks.body: At a clinic, the person giving the injection wears the “doer” badge and the patient wears the “receiver” badge. Pronouns work the same way: a doer gets I, we, he, she, they or who; a receiver (after a verb or after to, for, with or between) gets me, us, him, her, them or whom. A coworker standing beside you in a pair does not change your badge: cover them up and see which badge you need alone.

blocks.text: “Myself” is not a third badge for sounding polite. It only works when the same person is the doer earlier in the clause: “I reminded myself.”

explain.body: Subjects take I, we, he, she, they. Objects of verbs and prepositions take me, us, him, her, them. With a pair, drop the other noun and read the pronoun alone.

test.q: Which pronoun correctly completes the sentence? “Ms. Vega and ___ will proctor the anatomy exam on Friday.”
test.why: The pair is the subject of “will proctor.” Drop test: “I will proctor,” so “Ms. Vega and I.”

whyNot.2: “Myself” needs an I earlier in the clause to reflect.
whyNot.3: “Her will proctor” fails: “her” is objective; the subject form is “she.”

explain.body: Between, for, with, to, of and by are prepositions. Every pronoun after them is an object, even when a second person is in the pair: between you and me, for Dev and her, with Ana and them.

test.q: Which phrase correctly completes the sentence? “The preceptor divided the six patients between ___.”
test.why: “Between” is a preposition, so both of its objects take the objective case: “between Tomas and me.”

whyNot.0: “I” is subjective; after a preposition the objective “me” is needed.
whyNot.2: “Myself” has no I in the clause to reflect.
whyNot.3: “I” is still subjective, and it is the wrong case after “between.”

explain.body: Rewrite the pronoun's own clause as a statement and swap in he or him. He means who; him means whom. Only the pronoun's job inside its own clause matters.

test.q: Which word correctly completes the question? “___ is responsible for the supply order this week?”
test.why: The pronoun is the subject of “is responsible” (he is responsible), so the subjective “Who” is correct.

whyNot.1: “Whom” is objective (him) and cannot be the subject of “is.”
whyNot.2: “Whose” shows possession and would need a noun after it (whose team).
whyNot.3: “Whomever” is objective and does not begin a direct question.

explain.body: A reflexive (myself, herself, themselves) needs its own antecedent in the same clause. Possessive pronouns (hers, its, yours, theirs) never take an apostrophe; it's always means it is or it has.

test.q: Which sentence uses a reflexive pronoun correctly?
options: The twins taught theirselves to swim.
Dana and myself will lead the tour.
The patient fed himself at lunch today.
Please give the keys to Jo or myself.
test.why: “Himself” reflects “the patient,” the subject of the same clause.

whyNot.1: “Myself” cannot be part of a subject; use “Dana and I.”
whyNot.3: “Myself” has no I to reflect; after “to,” use “me.”
